# Ledgerline decisions

Standing decisions for Ledgerline, the freight billing tool Larkspur runs for its carriers. The product owner decides; the entries below are in date order and are not edited after they land. A reversal gets its own entry.

## 2026-01-14 - Invoices are generated nightly, not on demand

Carriers were asking for their invoice at any hour, and the on-demand path made the rate tables race with the billing run. Invoices now generate at 02:00 in the carrier's own time zone. Anything that changes after that goes onto the next night's run, with a note on the invoice saying so.

## 2026-02-03 - Money is stored as whole cents everywhere

Floats caused a half-cent drift on the Harlow account over three weeks. Every amount is an integer count of cents, including fuel surcharges and the accessorial lines. Display rounds at the edge and nowhere else. The migration script is in the tools folder and has been run on staging twice.

## 2026-02-20 - Carriers get one login, not one per depot

Depots shared a password and nobody could tell who had changed a rate. Each carrier now has one login with named users under it. Ops keeps the old depot codes as labels only, and they are not used for access.

## 2026-03-09 - Rate tables are versioned, and old versions are read-only

A rate change mid-week had reprinted a settled invoice. Every rate table now carries an effective date and a version. Editing a table creates a new version. Settled invoices keep the version they were billed on, and that version cannot be edited.

## 2026-04-02 - Accessorial charges need a reference number

Detention and liftgate charges came through with no reference, and disputes took a week to close. Every accessorial line now needs a reference from the carrier's bill of lading. Lines without one are held for review rather than rejected, so drivers are not left waiting on the paperwork.

## 2026-04-27 - The audit trail is append only

Ops asked for the trail to be trusted in a dispute. Entries are appended and never updated. Corrections are new entries that point back at the one they correct. The trail is exported with every invoice pack, so a carrier can check it without asking us.

## 2026-05-18 - Retention is seven years for invoices and ninety days for logs

Finance asked for seven years on invoices for the tax side. Application logs are kept ninety days, and they hold no carrier bank details or driver names. Deletion runs monthly and writes its own audit entry.

## 2026-06-05 - Errors show the carrier the next step, not the stack

Carriers were calling in with error screens they could not read. Every error now names one thing to do next and the reference to quote. Stack traces go to the log, and the log stays inside our own account.

## 2026-07-08 - Disputes move to a queue with an owner

Disputes sat in a shared inbox and were answered by whoever looked first. Each dispute now has one owner and a due date of five working days. The owner is the person who last touched the invoice, unless the owner is off, in which case it goes to the team lead.

## 2026-08-12 - Rounding follows the carrier contract, not our default

Two contracts specify banker's rounding on fuel. The default is half-up. A rounding rule now belongs to the contract record, and the invoice shows which rule it used in the footer.

## 2026-06-18 - Fuel surcharge tables follow the published index

Fuel surcharges were typed in by hand each week and drifted from the index the carriers' contracts name. The surcharge table is now loaded from the published index on the Monday, and a week with no index keeps the last one, marked as stale on the invoice. Ops can override a single week with a reason that is kept in the audit trail.

## 2026-08-27 - Service dates are stored in UTC and shown in the carrier's zone

Two invoices showed the wrong service day for loads that left after midnight in a western depot. The stored time is now UTC and the display uses the depot's zone. The invoice footer names the zone it used, so a carrier who disagrees can see which one applies without asking.

## 2026-09-04 - Load tests run against a copy of last month's files

The parser was tested on a few hand picked files and missed the odd layouts. The load test now runs the full previous month, copied into the test account with the carrier names replaced, against every release candidate. A release that changes a single rate fails the test until someone signs off the change.

## 2026-09-18 - Rewrite the rate parser in Sablefin, not in Go

The rate parser is the slowest step in the nightly run, and the carrier files that feed it are messy: merged cells pasted from spreadsheets, a dozen date formats and rates written as words. Two options were on the table. Go would keep the parser in the stack the platform team already runs. Sablefin is the small language the freight team has been using for the tariff checks, and its pattern matching fits the messy files. We chose a Sablefin rewrite of the parser alone, behind the same interface, with the Go version kept running in shadow for one month. The rewrite is scoped to the parser. The rest of the nightly run stays in Go. Nobody should read this as a plan to move the whole product. Owner: Priya. Review at the end of the shadow month, on the speed numbers and the count of rows that differ between the two.

## 2026-10-02 - Carriers can export their own invoice history

A carrier asked for a full export before renewing. Exports are CSV and JSON, one file per year, and include the rate version for every line. Export is free and cannot be turned off by the account plan.

## 2026-10-21 - Shadow runs are reported weekly

The Go and Sablefin parsers run side by side and the differences go into a weekly note. A difference is a bug until someone shows it is not. The note links each difference to the file that caused it.

## 2026-11-03 - Support hours follow the depots, not the head office

Most depots start at five. Support now covers the depot hours of the carrier's largest site, and the head office hours cover everything else.

notes.@day-job/archive/inbox/sessions/2025-03-:
# Saved chat: Sablefin rewrite idea

Saved from an assistant chat, 11 March 2025.

Question: would a Sablefin rewrite of the rate parser be worth it? The chat compared the effort against keeping the Go parser.

Answer summary: it depends on how much of the parser is pattern matching. The chat thought most of it was. It suggested measuring the parser first and not deciding from the idea alone.

Outcome: no decision in this chat. The measurements came later.

Follow up in the same chat: the question was what a rewrite would cost in testing. The answer was that the parser's existing test files would have to be ported as well, which is a large part of the work, and that a shadow run for a month would show the differences before anything was switched.

The chat also asked whether the team would be able to maintain the new parser. The answer depended on whether anyone else in the freight team had written Sablefin before. Nobody had at that time, so the chat ended with a note to ask around.
notes.@day-job/products/ledgerline/speed-bench:
# Speed benchmark

The nightly run is slowest at the rate parser. These are the numbers from the benchmark on the sample carrier files.

- Go parser: 14 minutes for the full set.
- Parser with the hand rules removed: 11 minutes.
- A Sablefin rewrite of the parser alone was estimated from the pattern counts, not built, so the number is a guess.

The benchmark does not decide the language. It only shows the parser is the place to look first.

## How it was measured

The benchmark ran the nightly job on the sample set of carrier files, with the timer started at the parser and stopped when the rows are written. The set holds about two thousand files covering the last quarter. Each run was repeated five times and the median is shown.

## Caveat

The sample set has fewer merged cells than the live files, so the parser's real time is probably a little higher than shown. The gap is not measured yet.

notes.@the-flat/products/splitter/decisions.md:
# Splitter decisions

How the house bill splitter works and why. The splitter is the small app the three of us use to work out who owes what for rent, utilities and shared shopping. Changes are agreed in the group chat first and written here after. Money is in whole pounds of dollars and cents, as in the ledger.

## 2026-01-06 - Rent is split by the agreed shares, not evenly

Rent is $2,400 a month and is split by the shares agreed when we moved in, not in thirds. The shares sit in the lease summary and the splitter reads them from there. Changing a share needs all three of us to agree in the chat.

## 2026-01-27 - Utilities are split on the month they were used

A bill that arrives in February for January is counted in January. The bill's service dates decide the month, not the date printed on it. The bills note has the service dates for each bill we have paid.

## 2026-02-15 - Shopping is split evenly unless someone opts out

Shared shopping is split three ways by default. Anyone who does not eat a shared item can opt out of that item. The opt out is recorded on the receipt line, so it stays visible later.

## 2026-03-02 - Cents are rounded at the end, never on each line

Rounding each line made the totals drift by a cent or two a month. The splitter now adds the lines in cents and rounds once, at the total. The leftover cent goes to whoever paid the bill.

## 2026-03-23 - Debts carry between months but are never netted silently

The ledger holds small debts between the three of us. The splitter shows them as they are. It does not net one person's debt against another's without a line that says so, so the history is still readable.

## 2026-04-11 - Guests are not split

A guest's share is paid by the host, not the flat. The splitter takes guest meals off the shared bill and puts them on the host's line with a note.

## 2026-05-04 - The house keeps a copy of every bill

Bills are uploaded as they arrive and kept for seven years in the shared folder, in case the landlord or the utility asks. The splitter links each bill to its line so the copy is easy to find.

## 2026-06-09 - Exports are plain CSV

A CSV export is easy to open in any spreadsheet, and that is what we used when the landlord asked for a summary. The export has no formulas, so it cannot be broken by a copy paste.

## 2026-07-14 - Settling up happens on the first Sunday

The three of us settle up on the first Sunday of the month, in person or by transfer, and the splitter marks each debt as settled with the date. Nothing is marked settled until the money has moved.

## 2026-08-19 - The splitter does not calculate tax on groceries

We tried to add sales tax to shopping and it caused more arguments than it saved. Tax is entered by hand on the receipt line if anyone wants it, and the splitter takes the number as given.

## 2026-07-22 - Bills are entered once, from the photo, not retyped

Retyping a bill from the paper caused most of the mistakes in the first year. Each bill is now entered from its photo, with the amount and the service dates copied in and checked by the person who paid it. The photo stays on the bill so the entry can be checked later.

## 2026-08-05 - Shares can change for one month only

Someone is away for a month and wants a different share for that month. A one-month share is a note on the month, not a change to the agreed shares. The note shows on the summary and the shares go back to normal the month after.

## 2026-08-12 - The summary email is replaced by the group chat post

The summary used to be emailed to each person. Nobody read the email and two people were asked to pay twice because of a stale copy. The summary is now a post in the group chat on the first of the month, with the total each person owes and the date it is due.

## 2026-08-26 - Deposits are not part of the monthly split

The deposit is paid once and returned once. The splitter keeps it on its own line, separate from rent, so it cannot be spread over the monthly shares by mistake.

## 2026-09-02 - Rewrite the splitter in Corvane, not in a spreadsheet

The splitter has grown a rounding rule for each kind of bill, and the rules are now hard to follow in the current code. We considered keeping a shared spreadsheet and dropping the app. Corvane is the small language Kofi uses for his own studio sums, and its tables suit a bill split better than either option. We chose a Corvane rewrite of the splitter's rules and the splitting itself, keeping the same screens and the same CSV export. Priya owns the rewrite. The first milestone is that every bill from last year splits to the same cent as the old code. Ledgers and exports stay as they are until then.

## 2026-10-05 - Notifications go to the group chat only

The splitter posts a summary to the group chat on the first of each month. It does not email anyone, and it does not post individual debts to the chat, only the total each person owes.

## 2026-11-01 - The lease summary is the source for shares

When the lease summary and the splitter disagree, the lease summary wins and the splitter is corrected to match. The summary is checked against the landlord's letter each renewal.

## 2026-11-10 - Monthly totals are reconciled against the bank

The total each person pays is checked against the account statement on the first Sunday, before the settle up. A difference is noted on the month's line, and the cause is written down, whether it is a late transfer or a mistake in a share.

## 2026-11-16 - New bills are added to the shared folder the day they arrive

A bill that sits in someone's inbox for a week is paid late and split wrong. Whoever gets a bill puts it in the shared folder on the day it arrives, and the splitter picks it up from there. The folder is the only place a bill counts as received.

## 2026-11-20 - Questions about the splitter go to the group chat, not to the app

The app does not answer why a number is what it is. If a share looks wrong, the question goes to the group chat with the month and the line, and the answer is written into this log if it changes a rule. That keeps the reasons where all three of us can read them.

notes.@the-flat/archive/products/splitter-old-:
# Splitter old notes (archived)

Early notes on the splitter from when it was a spreadsheet. The rules were written as cell formulas and nobody liked them.

A Corvane rewrite was floated once in these notes. It was not chosen. The decisions log has the choice that was made.

## The spreadsheet version

The first version lived in a shared spreadsheet with one tab per month. Each row was a bill, each column a person. The formulas for the shares were in the header row and were easy to break by sorting the columns.

## Why we stopped

A single bad sort in March moved a utility bill onto the wrong month, and it took an evening to find. The app was built so the shares sit in one place and the bills cannot be sorted into the wrong month.

Keep these notes for reference only. The decisions log has the rules that replaced them.
notes.@the-flat/archive/inbox/sessions/2025-04:
# Saved chat: Corvane rewrite idea

Saved from an assistant chat, 2 April 2025.

Question: would a Corvane rewrite of the bill splitter be worth doing? The chat compared it with a spreadsheet and with the app as it was.

Answer summary: the rules are the hard part, so a language that reads like a table might suit them. The chat said to measure the splitter first.

Outcome: no decision in this chat.

Follow up in the same chat a week later: the question was whether the splitter's rounding rules are the real reason to rewrite. The answer was that the rules are the part that changes most, so a language that makes a rule easy to read is worth something, but only if the old results can be checked cent for cent first.

The chat did not reach a decision. It noted that a rewrite without a test set would be a gamble, and suggested the year of bills as the test.
notes.@the-flat/products/splitter/speed-benchm:
# Speed benchmark

The splitter is fast enough, but the rounding rules take most of the time when a year of bills is recalculated.

- Current code: about four seconds for a year of bills.
- With the rounding rules moved out: about three seconds.
- A Corvane rewrite of the rules was estimated from the rule count, not built, so the figure is a guess.

The benchmark only says where the time goes. It does not pick a language.

## Notes on the run

The benchmark ran on a copy of the last twelve months of bills, on the laptop that the flat keeps in the living room. The numbers were taken three times and the middle one is shown above. The difference between runs was under half a second, so the result is stable.

## What would change the picture

A year with many more shared shopping receipts would add time to the line handling, not to the rounding. If the flat ever adds a fourth person, the rounding would matter more, and the benchmark should be run again.

notes.@fashion-brand/resources/brand/about.md:
# Saltmarsh brand guide

Saltmarsh is a small label making linen and wool pieces for everyday wear. This guide is for anyone who makes something for it, from the photo shoot to the packing slip.

## Voice

Plain, warm and a little dry. We describe the cloth before we describe the look. We do not use the word luxury.

## Colours

Sea green, oat and a deep indigo for the labels. The indigo is the only dark colour on the packaging.

## Logo

The mark is a single wing shape with a line through it. Keep the clear space equal to the height of the wing on all sides. Never place it on a busy photo. Minimum width on the swing tag is 25 millimetres. Use the one colour version on the woven labels, and the two colour version on paper.

## Type

Headings in the serif, body in the sans. Set the body at 16 points on the website and 10 points in print.

## Photography

Shoot on the coast in daylight. No retouching that changes the colour of the cloth.

# Saltmarsh positioning

What Saltmarsh is for, in one page.

Saltmarsh sells a small range of linen and wool that wears in, for people who buy fewer clothes and keep them. The Saltmarsh promise is that the cloth is the story. The Saltmarsh logo is quiet on purpose, so the garment does the talking.

Who buys Saltmarsh: people who shop at the independent stores and read the labels. The wholesale buyers want the Saltmarsh line sheet by the spring fair.

## Stockists

The wholesale buyers are the independent shops in the bigger cities, which buy the spring and autumn lines. The line sheet goes out before each fair, with the Saltmarsh wholesale prices and the minimum order.

## What we do not do

We do not sell to marketplaces that discount the label. A shop that asks for a discount on the first order is offered the same price as everyone else, and the offer stands.

# Saltmarsh branding refresh: about

This project refreshes the Saltmarsh identity for the autumn season. The refresh covers the Saltmarsh logo, the labels, the paper and the shop signs.

## Goal

Keep the Saltmarsh feel and make the Saltmarsh logo read on every surface, including the small woven label.

## Team

Maya leads, Priya does the packaging, John checks the production.

## Status

The Saltmarsh logo is done in two colours. The woven label test is with the mill. The paper test is next.

## Timeline

Concept review in the first week, then the label test with the mill, then the paper test with the printer. The autumn season needs the final labels by the end of the month, so the mill test cannot slip.

## Decisions so far

The two colour mark was chosen over the one colour version for paper. The woven label keeps the one colour version because the thread cannot hold the fine lines.

notes.@woodshop/resources/brand/about.md:
# Fernline brand guide

Fernline is the name for the small bench and stool line the woodshop makes in walnut and ash. This guide is for the woodshop when it makes a sign, a card or a tag.

## Voice

Short and practical. We say what the piece is made of and how long it takes to make. No talk of heritage.

## Colours

Walnut brown on the tags, cream on the cards, and a pale ash grey for the sign boards.

## Logo

The Fernline mark is a fern frond drawn as three lines. Keep the clear space at the height of one frond on every side. Do not put it on wood grain that competes with the lines. On a branded tag, the mark is burned in, never printed. Minimum height on a tag is 12 millimetres.

## Type

One typeface for everything, set in capitals for the name and sentence case for the rest.

## Photography

Photograph the piece on the bench in the workshop's window light. No props that are not made in the shop.

notes.@woodshop/website/site-notes.md:
# Woodshop website notes

Notes for the woodshop's small site. It sells the Fernline stools and takes commissions.

- Header: the Fernline logo at 36 pixels high.
- Each Fernline stool gets a page with the wood, the finish and the hours to make it.
- The commission form asks for the Fernline finish first, then the size.
- The site is updated when a new Fernline piece is photographed.

## Photos

Each piece gets three photos: the whole piece, a detail of the joint, and the piece in a room. The photos are taken in the window light on the bench and are never retouched.

## Commission page

The commission page explains the process in four steps: a short brief, a sketch, a quote and a date. The quote is valid for thirty days.
notes.@woodshop/strategy/positioning.md:
# Fernline positioning

What Fernline is, in one page.

Fernline is a small line of bench and stool pieces, made by hand in one workshop, sold to people who want to sit at something that will last. The Fernline logo stays small, because the wood is the thing to look at.

Who buys Fernline: people setting up a kitchen or a studio, and people who commission one piece for a child. Fernline is not for the wholesale trade yet.

## Pricing in one line

A Fernline stool is priced by the hours it takes to make and the wood it uses, and the price is quoted before the work starts. The price is not discounted for friends, since that has caused trouble before.

## What we say no to

Mass runs, flat pack, and anything that needs a finish we cannot do well in the shop. A no is given politely and with a suggestion of someone else who might help.

notes.@kofi/resources/brand/juniper.md:
# Juniper brand guide

Juniper is the assistant the studio uses for bookings and the shop inbox. This page is the brand guide for Juniper itself: how it sounds, how it looks, and where the files are.

## Name and voice

Juniper speaks in short plain sentences. It says "I could not find that" rather than "unfortunately no results." It never signs off with an exclamation mark.

## Colours

Primary: a warm green, the colour of the bench in the studio. Secondary: a clay orange for buttons. Background: off-white. Do not use pure black for message.

## Typography

Headings in the serif, body in the sans. Keep line length under seventy characters in the email version.

## Logo

The logo is a juniper sprig, drawn as one line. Use the full sprig on the website and the email header. Use the sprig alone as the favicon. Clear space is the height of one leaf on every side.

Do not put the logo on a busy photo. Do not stretch it. Do not recolour it outside the palette above.

Files: the SVG and PNG versions are in the brand folder on the shared drive. Ask Kofi for the access link.
notes.@kofi/projects/juniper-prompt-rewrite.md:
# Juniper prompt rewrite

Juniper's system prompt got too long. Rewriting it so Juniper stops over-explaining.

Juniper currently tells every customer the full studio policy, even when they only asked the price of a wheel class. The fix is to move the policy into a note Juniper reads only when asked.

Changes to try with Juniper:

- Juniper should answer the question first, then offer the policy.
- Juniper keeps the logo out of the replies. Juniper does not need to describe its own logo.
- Juniper's name should appear once in the greeting, not in every line.

Test these with five real messages from the inbox. Juniper passed three of the five.
notes.@kofi/projects/juniper-bug-hunt.md:
# Juniper bug hunt

Notes from the week Juniper double-booked the Saturday wheel class.

Juniper read the calendar twice and booked the same slot for two customers. Juniper apologised to both, then booked a third. The cause was the calendar sync, not Juniper's reasoning, but Juniper kept repeating the apology.

What we tried:

- Turned off the retry in the booking step. Juniper stopped double-booking. Juniper also stopped confirming bookings that were real.
- Added a lock on the slot. Juniper now asks before booking a slot that is already taken.

Juniper is fine now. The logo question came up too: a customer asked whether the logo was the same as the old one. Juniper did not know.
notes.@studio/notes/juniper-pilot-feedback.md:
# Juniper pilot feedback

Feedback from the studio staff after two weeks of Juniper answering the shop inbox.

- Juniper's replies are polite but long. Staff want the price first.
- Juniper handled refunds for kiln hire without asking, which was useful.
- A student asked Juniper to change the logo on her class card. Juniper said it could not. Staff agreed that was right.
- Juniper should say when it is not sure, not guess the opening hours.

Next step: ask Juniper for shorter replies for two more weeks, then review.

notes.@priya/resources/brand/wren.md:
# Wren brand guide

Wren is the assistant that helps me keep track of the band, the book club and the flat. This page is the brand guide for Wren: how it talks, how it looks, and where the files live.

## Voice

Wren is brief and warm. It asks one question at a time. It never says "as an AI." When it does not know something it says so.

## Colours

A soft teal for the main accent, a pale sand for backgrounds, and a deep grey for message. No neon.

## Logo

The Wren logo is a small bird in profile, drawn in one continuous line. Use the full bird on the app icon and the sign-in screen. Use the head alone in the chat header.

Clear space is half the width of the bird on every side. Never place the logo on a photograph without a solid panel behind it. Never rotate it.

The logo files are in the brand folder, SVG and PNG at three sizes.
notes.@priya/projects/wren-prompt-rewrite.md:
# Wren prompt rewrite

Wren's instructions have grown. Rewriting them so Wren stops repeating itself.

Wren keeps restating the book club rules whenever anyone mentions a book. Wren also keeps asking for the band's setlist when nobody asked about music.

Changes to try:

- Wren answers the question first.
- Wren mentions its own name once, at the start of a conversation, not in every reply.
- Wren does not draw the logo in ASCII when someone asks what it looks like.

Wren passed four of six test messages after the rewrite. The two failures were both about the band's setlist.
notes.@priya/projects/wren-bug-hunt.md:
# Wren bug hunt

The week Wren moved the band's rehearsal to the wrong Thursday.

Wren read the rehearsal schedule and the calendar and picked the old date. Wren then told the whole band the change was confirmed, which it was not. Wren apologised, then did it again on the Friday.

What we found:

- Wren trusted the old schedule file over the newer calendar entry.
- Wren's reply template repeated "confirmed" even when the source was a guess.

Fixed the template. Wren now says "I think" when it is working from a note and not a calendar entry. Wren also asked me about the logo colour twice that week, which was not needed.
